title: 2 Kings 1:9–18
context: Ahaziah, knowing the prophet is Elijah, sends a captain of fifty with his fifty. The captain finds Elijah sitting on the top of the hill and says, “Man of God, the king has said, ‘Come down!’” Elijah answers, “If I am a man of God, then let fire come down from the sky and consume you and your fifty!” Fire comes down from the sky and consumes the captain and his fifty. A second captain is sent and says, “Come down quickly!” Elijah gives the same answer; this time the narrator says, “Then God’s fire came down from the sky, and consumed him and his fifty.” The third captain comes, falls on his knees, and begs that his life and the lives of his fifty may be precious in Elijah’s sight, naming the fire that has already consumed the first two companies. The LORD’s angel then says to Elijah, “Go down with him. Don’t be afraid of him.” Elijah goes down and speaks the same word to the king: because he has sent to inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, as if there were no God in Israel, he will not come down from the bed, but will surely die. “So he died according to the LORD’s word which Elijah had spoken.” Jehoram begins to reign in his place in the second year of Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, because Ahaziah had no son. The rest of Ahaziah’s acts are referred to the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel, a court source named here and not simply to be identified with the later biblical book of that title. The fire is to be reported as the text gives it, without softening it, without dressing it up, and without being turned into a type. In Luke 9:54–55, James and John later ask, “Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from the sky and destroy them, just as Elijah did?” and Jesus turns and rebukes them. That later scene belongs to a different mission; it may be noted, but it does not rewrite this chapter, and it is not a contrast between the two traditions.

verses.text: Then the king sent a captain of fifty with his fifty to him. He went up to him; and behold, he was sitting on the top of the hill. He said to him, “Man of God, the king has said, ‘Come down!’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king sent a captain of fifty with his fifty. The captain went up, and “behold, he was sitting on the top of the hill.” He said, “Man of God, the king has said, ‘Come down!’” The title “Man of God” is in his mouth, but the order is the king’s: come down.

Arminian readers hear a real command, not a request. The company is armed in number, and the word from the king is to bring the prophet down.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the scene as a royal summons. Elijah sits on the hill; the captain speaks the king’s “Come down!”

Both traditions describe the approach as the narrator gives it. What follows is not yet told, and should not be read back as if the fire had already fallen.

verses.text: Elijah answered to the captain of fifty, “If I am a man of God, then let fire come down from the sky and consume you and your fifty!” Then fire came down from the sky, and consumed him and his fifty.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elijah answered, “If I am a man of God, then let fire come down from the sky and consume you and your fifty!” Then fire came down from the sky, and consumed him and his fifty. The answer takes up the title he has been given, and the fire comes down as he has said.

Arminian readers let the verse be as stark as it is. The fire falls on this captain and his fifty, and the text does not pause to soften or to explain the scene away. In a later mission, James and John will ask whether to command fire from the sky “just as Elijah did”, and they will be rebuked; that later word should not be used here to rewrite what this verse reports.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse both sanitizing and spectacle. “Then fire came down from the sky, and consumed him and his fifty.” is the narrator’s own sentence.

Both traditions report the event as it is given, without forced typology and without a party contrast over prophetic authority.

verses.text: Again he sent to him another captain of fifty with his fifty. He answered him, “Man of God, the king has said, ‘Come down quickly!’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Again the king sent another captain of fifty with his fifty. He answered him, “Man of God, the king has said, ‘Come down quickly!’” The second summons is sharper only in the added word “quickly”. The king has not changed his demand after the first fire.

Arminian readers hear a second, still free, act of the same policy. The new captain knows, or soon says, the same title and the same order, now with haste.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the king’s persistence. Another fifty are sent, and the word is, “Come down quickly!”

Both traditions take the verse as a second royal attempt, reported without comment, before Elijah answers again.

verses.text: Elijah answered them, “If I am a man of God, then let fire come down from the sky and consume you and your fifty!” Then God’s fire came down from the sky, and consumed him and his fifty.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elijah answered them, “If I am a man of God, then let fire come down from the sky and consume you and your fifty!” Then God’s fire came down from the sky, and consumed him and his fifty. The answer is the same; the narrator now says “God’s fire”.

Arminian readers again refuse to dress the scene up or to explain it away. A second company is consumed, and the wording “God’s fire” names whose fire it is, without turning the event into a type.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the small change in the narrative phrase: not only fire, but “God’s fire”, came down from the sky and consumed him and his fifty.

Both traditions report this second fall of fire as the text gives it, still without a forced typological contrast and without a dispute over the prophet’s authority as a party issue.

verses.text: Again he sent the captain of a third fifty with his fifty. The third captain of fifty went up, and came and fell on his knees before Elijah, and begged him, and said to him, “Man of God, please let my life and the life of these fifty of your servants be precious in your sight.
verses.arminianNotes:
A third captain of fifty is sent. He went up, “came and fell on his knees before Elijah, and begged him,” and said, “Man of God, please let my life and the life of these fifty of your servants be precious in your sight”. The speech continues into the next verse. The title is the same; the posture and the plea are not.

Arminian readers hear a real change in this captain’s approach. He kneels, he begs, he calls the fifty “your servants”, and he asks that their lives be precious.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise mark the difference without inventing a speech the text does not give. The third captain falls on his knees and pleads for his life and for theirs.

Both traditions describe this third coming as the narrator does, and they wait for the plea to be finished in verse 14.

verses.text: Behold, fire came down from the sky and consumed the last two captains of fifty with their fifties. But now let my life be precious in your sight.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He continues, “Behold, fire came down from the sky and consumed the last two captains of fifty with their fifties. But now let my life be precious in your sight.” He names what has happened and asks again that his life be precious.

Arminian readers hear an honest confession of the facts and a plea, not a new command from the king. He does not repeat “Come down!” He asks to be spared.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same turn. The fire on the first two companies is acknowledged, and the request is for life to be treated as precious.

Both traditions take the finished plea as the reason the next word, from the LORD’s angel, can send Elijah down without fear.

verses.text: The LORD’s angel said to Elijah, “Go down with him. Don’t be afraid of him.” Then he arose and went down with him to the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s angel said to Elijah, “Go down with him. Don’t be afraid of him.” Then he arose and went down with him to the king. The descent happens only when the angel says to go and not to fear.

Arminian readers hear a new word, not a change forced by the king. Elijah goes down with this captain because the LORD’s angel tells him to, and he is told not to be afraid of him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise place the authority in the angel’s sentence: “Go down with him. Don’t be afraid of him.” Elijah arises and goes.

Both traditions read the verse as the turning of the scene from the hill to the sick king. The later rebuke in Luke 9:54–55, already noted, belongs to another mission and does not unsettle this command to go down.

verses.text: He said to him, “The LORD says, ‘Because you have sent messengers to inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, is it because there is no God in Israel to inquire of his word? Therefore you will not come down from the bed where you have gone up, but you will surely die.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Elijah said to him, “The LORD says, ‘Because you have sent messengers to inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, is it because there is no God in Israel to inquire of his word? Therefore you will not come down from the bed where you have gone up, but you will surely die.’ ” The word first sent through the messengers is now spoken to the king’s face, with the added clause “to inquire of his word”.

Arminian readers hear the same charge and the same sentence, now delivered in person. The king’s sending is the reason named, and the outcome is not altered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the LORD’s word has not shifted. The inquiry of Baal Zebub, as if there were no God in Israel whose word could be sought, remains the ground, and the death sentence is repeated.

Both traditions take this as the public confirmation of verses 3–4, spoken to Ahaziah himself.

verses.text: So he died according to the LORD’s word which Elijah had spoken. Jehoram began to reign in his place in the second year of Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, because he had no son.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So he died according to the LORD’s word which Elijah had spoken.” Jehoram began to reign in his place “in the second year of Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, because he had no son.” The death matches the word. Two men named Jehoram appear in the synchronism, one in Israel and one in Judah.

Arminian readers take the death as the word fulfilled, and they leave the dating as the narrator states it. Harmonies of the two Jehorams and the year-counts in Kings are discussed elsewhere and should not be settled by a guess in this verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep the fulfillment central: he died according to the LORD’s word which Elijah had spoken. The second year of Jehoram of Judah is the book’s own notice, given because Ahaziah had no son.

Both traditions report the succession as it is written, without inventing a chronological scheme the passage does not explain.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Ahaziah which he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now the rest of the acts of Ahaziah which he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?” The formula closes the reign by pointing to a royal record.

Arminian readers hear a standard close, not a direction to the later biblical book of Chronicles as such. The court source named here is not simply to be identified with that book.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the question as the usual ending of a king’s account in this history. The rest of Ahaziah’s acts are said to be written in that chronicle of the kings of Israel.

Both traditions close the chapter there, with the word fulfilled and the reign ended, and without a party contrast over what has been told.
